title: Half Steps and Whole Steps
description: The two smallest moves on the keyboard, and the only two places white keys sit right next to each other.

steps.title: The smallest step
steps.description:
A semitone, or half step, is the smallest move you can make on a piano: from one key to the very next one, black or white. Two semitones make a tone, or whole step.

Every scale you'll ever play is just a mix of these two moves.

steps.title: C to C#
steps.description: Play C and the black key right next to it, C#, together. That's one semitone. Close together like this, they grind against each other a bit.
steps.hint: Middle C and the black key just to its right.

steps.title: E to F
steps.description: Now E and F together. These are both white keys, but there's no black key between them, so this is a semitone too.
steps.hint: E is just right of the pair of black keys, and F is right next to it.

steps.title: C to D
steps.description: Play C and D together. There's a black key (C#) sitting between them, so this is two semitones, a whole step. It sounds more relaxed than the half step did.
steps.hint: Middle C and the next white key up. Skip over the black key.

steps.title: Where white keys touch
steps.description:
There are only two spots where two white keys are a half step apart, with no black key between them:

• E and F
• B and C

Every other pair of neighbouring white keys is a whole step. Those two gaps are why the black keys come in groups of two and three.

steps.title: B to C
steps.description: Here's the other one. Play B and the C just above it. No black key between them, so it's a half step.
steps.hint: The B just below C5 and the C right after it. B sits just right of the group of three black keys.

steps.title: Adding it up
steps.description: How many semitones make one whole step?
